1 GRAMMAR – The perfect aspect

  

    Find out: Perfect forms (have/has/had + past participle) link two times — for example a past action and its result now, or an action that continues up to a point. The continuous perfect (have been + -ing) stresses duration or an ongoing process.

2 / 3 VOCABULARY – Describing changes

  

    Interesting note: Languages change all the time — new words appear (neologisms), meanings shift, and some words become rare or obsolete. Describing change often uses verbs like spread, decline, evolve, replace and time markers like nowadays, formerly, over the last decade.
  



  

    
a Complete the text with the words in the box.

    
rapid changes   substantially   noticeable   way   barely   slight   increase   subtle   ongoing

    

      
Changes to the English language may not always be immediately , but because over 500 million people now use it as their first language, it is constantly evolving.

      
Some , often made in an attempt to simplify the language, are  perceptible. However, over time we notice that people are not using ‘ought to’ as much any more, and ‘right?’ is being used instead of question tags, which seem to be on the  out.

      
The use of Americanisms by British youth is clearly on the , with expressions such as, ‘Can I get a coffee to go?’ becoming very common. Interest in American TV programmes and music has grown  over the last 20 years, leading to a  rise in American usage.

      
Linguists and lexicographers spot the most  changes in the language and make decisions as to whether a steady  over time is enough to justify a new dictionary entry or even a change to a grammar rule.

2 These changes may have a hugely significant impact, but can go entirely unnoticed while they are in progress.

      
3 Here are some of the most noticeable changes that are occurring in English right now:

      
4 There was a steady shift towards more frequent use of the verb + -ing, and these forms are still on the increase.

Typical sentence stress falls on content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs). Function words are usually weak.

    5.

4 LISTENING AND GRAMMAR – The perfect aspect


  

    
a 01.10 Listen to four people commenting on the article in 2a and answer the questions.

    
    

      
🎧 Track 01.10 – Four speakers (Paul, Rosa, Greg, Claire)

      
      
    


    
    
      
  1. What kind of language change does each speaker focus on?
    2. 
      
  2. What specific examples does each speaker give?
    3. 
    

    
    
    
    

      
Paul – Speed of change / new words spreading fast because of the internet.

      Examples: LOL, BTW, wearable technology, cloud storage – many won’t last; in a few years they will have gone out of fashion.

      
Rosa – Punctuation and spelling (effect of texting and spell-checkers).

      Examples: people use commas much less; confuse lose/loose, affect/effect; spelling is getting worse.

      
Greg – Dialects disappearing / language becoming more uniform because of international communication.

      Examples: “movies” has replaced “cinema” and “film” worldwide; in about 50 years most dialects will have died out.

      
Claire – New words enrich the language; words change meaning (natural process).

      Examples: “selfie” (people had been taking photos of themselves before 2013 but had no single word); “wireless” used to mean radio, now means internet connection / Wi-Fi.

e 01.11 Pronunciation – Listen to the sentences in 4c again and notice the pronunciation of the underlined words. What kind of words are stressed? What kind of words are usually unstressed?

    
    
    

      Content words (main verbs, nouns, adjectives, adverbs) are usually stressed. Function words (auxiliaries like has, have, had, will, articles, prepositions) are usually unstressed / weak forms.

b Read the fact file and discuss the questions.

    
    
      
  1. What do you think each fact tells us about the speakers’ culture or environment? Or the way they think about the world?
    2. 
      
  2. Which language feature do you think is the most unusual?
    3. 
    

    

      
FACT FILE: HOW LANGUAGES ARE SPECIAL

      
The DANI OF NEW GUINEA only distinguish colours from one another using two words, one for dark colours and the other for light colours.

      
It is believed that the INUIT IN NORTHERN CANADA have about 50 different words for snow and about 40 ways to distinguish different kinds of ice from one another.

      
ALBANIAN has 27 different words for kinds of moustaches. Posht, for example, means a moustache that hangs down at the ends.

      
HAWAIIAN LANGUAGES have 108 words for sweet potato and 47 for banana.

      
In the NATIVE AMERICAN LANGUAGE HOPI, the verbs do not differentiate between past and present. Instead, the forms of its verbs convey how the speaker came to know the information.

      
GUUGU YIMITHIRR, a language spoken in northeast Australia, does not have words for ‘left’ and ‘right’ as directions at all. Instead, they use north, south, east and west. When they want someone to turn while driving, they’ll say, for example, ‘Turn a little bit west’.

      
In the language of the MARQUESAN ISLANDS, directions are indicated with reference to geographical features – which can make them hard to interpret if you don’t know exactly where you are. For example, a Marquesan might say that your bicycle is ‘downstream of the house’ or that you should ‘Walk inland, then seaward’ to get to your destination.

      
UNTRANSLATABLE

      
Most languages have unique words and idioms that are impossible to translate exactly. These words often embody the culture of the people who speak the language. Some examples that illustrate this:

      
    
        
  • ENGLISH: cosy – pleasantly warm and comfortable
    • 
        
  • GERMAN: fernweh – a longing to be somewhere far away
    • 
        
  • JAPANESE: mono no aware – a gentle sadness at the impermanence of things
    • 
        
  • DUTCH: uitwaaien – walking in windy weather for fun
    • 
        
  • GREEK: parea – a group of friends who meet to share ideas and experiences
    • 
        
  • KIVILA (PAPUA NEW GUINEA): mokita – the truth that everyone knows but nobody talks about
    •
